It's November 2031. Ludwig's knee has got worse. He struggles to climb up to the first floor. Mara has come with a suggestion.
Ludwig, I saw you on the stairs this morning. It took you five minutes for one floor.
The knee. It'll pass. It's not the first time I've climbed the stairs with a bad knee.
As a nurse I'm telling you: it won't get better. The ground-floor flat has been empty since the summer. You could move.
Move? Me? I've lived on the first floor for thirty-six years. I'm not moving!
You don't have to move far. Just one floor down. And we'd renovate the flat first: a wide bathroom, no steps, a window onto the courtyard.
And Ingrid's books? Her armchair? The whole life I've lived upstairs?
The books move with you. The armchair moves with you. And you don't lose your life just because you don't climb the stairs any more.
I have to think about it. I'm not deciding this today.
Of course not. But at least have a look at the flat. Jakob and I started taking off the old wallpaper yesterday.
You've already started? Without asking me?
The wallpaper had to come off anyway. And Jakob discovered something behind the wallpaper. Something you should see.
The stress changes the meaning: “OOM-fah-ren” (to knock down) / “oom-FAH-ren” (to drive around).
The prefixes be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer- never separate from the verb, are not stressed, and the participle doesn't take ge-:
Compare: kommen (to come) → bekommen (to get, to receive), entkommen (to escape), verkommen (to go to ruin). The prefix can change the meaning completely.
“bekommen” does NOT mean “to become”! “Ich bekomme ein Geschenk” = I get a present. “to become” = werden.
3. The two-way prefixes: um-, über-, durch-, wieder-
These prefixes can be separable (stressed, concrete meaning) or inseparable (unstressed, figurative meaning):
UMziehen: Ich ziehe um. (to move house)
UMfahren: Er fährt den Baum um. (to knock down)
umFAHren: Er umfährt den Stau. (to drive around)
WIEDERkommen: Er kommt wieder. (to come back)
wiederHOlen: Er wiederholt den Satz. (to repeat)
ÜBERsetzen: Die Fähre setzt über. (to cross the water)
überSETzen: Sie übersetzt den Brief. (to translate)
The participle: separable → umgezogen, wiedergekommen; inseparable → umarmt, wiederholt, übersetzt.
Learn verbs in families, because they're easier to remember that way:
to pull → to move (house), to put on (clothes), to take off (clothes) / to move out, to move in
to stand → to understand, to come into being, to get up, to pass (an exam)

The ground-floor flat looked as if a storm had passed through. All over the floor lay strips of old wallpaper, brown and yellow and with little flowers, which someone must have found pretty back in the seventies. Under the wallpaper was another layer of wallpaper, and under that yet another, like the annual rings of a tree. Jakob was standing on a ladder holding an old, rusty tin box. It was the size of a shoebox and painted with sailing ships.
It was hidden in the wall, behind the old tiled stove. There was a loose brick there. Someone hid it there on purpose. I didn't want to open it without you.

Mara brushed the dust off her hands and sat down on the windowsill. Jakob climbed down from the ladder and put the box carefully on the floor, as if it were made of glass. Outside in the courtyard, the November rain was falling on the old chestnut tree, which had lost almost all its leaves. It smelled of old paper, of lime plaster and of something else that Mara didn't recognise, something sweet, like cinnamon or like old sweets. “I only shook it a little,” Jakob admitted. “There's paper inside. And something hard.”

Ludwig sat down on an upturned bucket, because there wasn't a single chair, and put the box on his knees. The lid was stuck. It took him a whole minute to open it, and nobody helped him, because they all knew he wanted to do it himself. Then it opened, slowly, with a metallic sigh.

In the box there were: a school exercise book with a blue cover, a photo of a little girl with plaits in front of the house, a dried rose, a small piece of grey concrete with bright paint on one side, and a folded letter with the words: “To whoever finds this.” Ludwig took the letter. His hands were trembling a little, but not because of his age.

My name is Susanne Lehmann. I'm fourteen. Today is the 12th of November 1989. Three days ago the Wall fell. I broke off this piece myself, with my father's hammer, on Bernauer Straße. Next week we're moving to the West, to Hanover, to my aunt's. My parents say we'll have a better future there. I don't want to leave.

Ludwig stopped and took the piece of concrete out of the box. He turned it between his fingers. On one side it was grey and rough, on the other there were shining traces of red and yellow spray paint. “I was there too, that night,” he said quietly. “On the ninth of November. I drove my tram to Bornholmer Straße, and then I left the tram where it was, in the middle of the route, and walked across the bridge with everyone else. My boss never punished me for it afterwards. He had crossed too.”

I'm hiding this box here so that something of me stays in this house. This flat was the happiest place of my childhood. This is where I learned to read, this is where I got my first love letter, the rose is from him, his name is Mirko and he lives on the first floor. Whoever you are: please be happy here. As happy as I was.

Under the letter, in very small writing, there was something else: “PS: If you meet Mirko, tell him I kept his letter. But don't tell him I cried.” Mara laughed and cried at the same time. Jakob cleared his throat and looked out of the window, the way men do when they don't want to show they're moved.

It was quiet in the flat. Outside a tram went by. Mara had put her hand over her mouth. Jakob slowly climbed down from the ladder. Ludwig read the letter twice, then a third time, then put it carefully back in the box.

Ludwig said quietly: “On the first floor. In my flat. Mirko lived in my flat.” He looked up at the ceiling, as if he could see through it his own living room, the armchair, the bookshelves, the window onto the street. “I lived there for thirty-six years and never knew that a boy in that room wrote a love letter to a girl who lived two metres below him.”

Susanne Lehmann. I've never heard the name. When I took over the building in 1995, other people were already living here. But I remember the tiled stove. The previous owner wanted to remove it, and Ingrid said: No, it stays. A house needs a heart. If we had destroyed it back then, nobody would ever have discovered the box.

Meanwhile Jakob had taken out his phone. “Susanne Lehmann, born in 1975, from Berlin, later Hanover,” he murmured. “There must be a hundred women.” But Mara took the blue exercise book out of the box and leafed through it. On the last page, in a little girl's round handwriting, there was an address in Hanover and below it, added later, with a different pen: “If I come back: I'm going to be a teacher.”
Outside, the front door slammed, and Fritz gave one short bark on the stairs, as if he wanted to ask why nobody was paying any attention to him today.
A teacher called Susanne Lehmann, about fifty-six. We'll find her. Michael is a teacher, he knows people in every school authority. Ludwig, may I?

Jakob looked up: “And Mirko? We should look for him too. Mirko from the first floor. How many Mirkos can there be in Berlin who were about fourteen or fifteen in 1989?” “More than you think,” said Ludwig. “Lots of boys were called that back then. But maybe there's something in the exercise book.” Mara leafed on. On one page, between maths exercises and a drawing of a horse, it said in small letters: “Mirko Petrović. Wants to be a musician. Plays the guitar, but badly.”

Ludwig nodded. Then he stood up, slowly, leaning on his walking stick, and for the first time really walked through the flat. He saw the window onto the courtyard, where the old chestnut tree stood, whose crown he had only ever seen from above for thirty-six years. He saw the tiled stove with its green tiles, where Susanne had probably warmed her hands as a child. He saw the wall behind which a secret had waited almost forty-two years, for him.

And he saw himself, a few months from now, in this room, in Ingrid's armchair by the window onto the courtyard, with Fritz on his feet and a cup of tea. No stairs. No more of those five long minutes every morning, holding on to the banister and pretending it was nothing. He thought of Ingrid, who always said you have to know when to let go. He had never understood what she meant. Maybe he understood now.
Mara. How long do you need to renovate the flat?
Two months, maybe three. Does that mean…?

It means I'm moving. In February. Susanne wrote that I have to be happy here. You don't contradict a fourteen-year-old girl who broke open the Wall with her father's hammer. But the tiled stove stays. A house needs a heart.

Mara hugged him so tightly that he almost dropped his walking stick. Jakob brought the ladder back and, without saying a word, began tearing the last of the wallpaper off the wall, faster than before. And Ludwig sat down on the bucket again, took the blue exercise book on his knees and began to read, from the first page, the story of a girl who had learned to read in this very room, almost fifty years ago. Outside the rain stopped. Through the window onto the courtyard a narrow strip of November sunlight fell on the tiled stove, and the green tiles shone, as if someone had lit the heart of the house again.
